inferred_prompt: Explain why switching doors in the Monty Hall problem doubles your chances of winning, in a way that makes the intuition clear.
style: general/lay audience, clear intuitive explanation, informal-educational register

responses.text: When you first pick a door, you have a one-in-three chance of choosing the car, which means the car sits behind one of the other two doors two-thirds of the time. Monty, who knows where the car is, then opens a losing door from that pair—but his reveal doesn't change your original odds; it just funnels that entire two-thirds probability onto the single remaining door. Switching, therefore, is like betting your first guess was wrong, which it usually was. Staying wins only when your initial one-in-three pick was lucky, so switching doubles your chances.

This doesn't change the original odds—it just concentrates that entire 2-in-3 probability onto the single remaining door. Switching effectively lets you bet on two doors instead of one, which is why it doubles your chances.

The key insight is that the host isn't acting randomly—he knows where the car is and deliberately always opens a door revealing a goat, never the prize. This means his action carries information. Think of it this way: two-thirds of the time you started by pointing at a goat, and in every one of those cases the host is forced to reveal the other goat, leaving the car sitting behind the one remaining unopened door. So whenever your first pick was wrong (which happens two out of three times), switching lands you squarely on the car. Only in the one-in-three scenario where you happened to pick the car first does switching hurt you. Since being initially wrong is twice as likely as being initially right, switching wins twice as often as staying. A helpful way to feel this intuitively is to imagine a hundred doors: you pick one, the host opens ninety-eight goats, and suddenly it's obvious the single door he pointedly avoided almost certainly hides the car. Switching simply lets you trade your unlikely first guess for the odds concentrated everywhere else.

To intuitively understand why switching doors in the Monty Hall problem doubles your probability of winning, examine your initial odds. Selecting one of the three closed doors gives you a one in three probability of picking the car, compared to a two in three probability of picking a goat. The secret is that Monty possesses total knowledge of what lies behind every door and is forced to reveal a goat. If you initially selected the car, which happens one out of three times, switching makes you lose. However, if you initially selected a goat, which happens two out of three times, Monty must reveal the only remaining goat on stage. That means the one unopened door remaining must conceal the car. Because you are twice as likely to pick a goat on your first try, switching automatically flips an incorrect choice into a winning one. By switching doors, you are simply betting your initial guess was incorrect, securing the car exactly two out of three times.
